Problem 850. Majority rule and a protected right: case 5
Democratic procedures use voting, but constitutional systems can place some rights beyond ordinary majority power.

A council of 29 members votes 20 to 9 for a proposal that would forbid one named group from the right to be protected from arbitrary punishment. The classroom constitution states: (1) ordinary proposals pass by simple majority; (2) an ordinary majority may not remove the listed equal rights from a group.
A decision must satisfy both the voting procedure and the higher rights constraint. Passing a vote is not sufficient if the content violates a protected right.
Did the proposal receive a majority? May it take effect under the stated constitution?

1. Vote check: 20>9, so the proposal has a simple majority. 2. Content check: the proposal removes a protected equal right (be protected from arbitrary punishment) from a group. 3. The higher rights rule therefore blocks the proposal even though the vote passed.
It received a majority, but it may not take effect under the stated rights rule.
A majority answers who won a vote; it does not by itself answer whether every possible decision is lawful or fair under higher rules.
Two-stage validity test: procedural predicate AND rights-compliance predicate.
Problem 851. Quorum and majority in a 23-member committee
Voting rules often contain more than one threshold. Quorum concerns participation; majority concerns the votes cast according to the stated rule.

A committee has 23 members. 23 are present. Votes: yes=11, no=11, abstain=1. Rule: quorum is at least 60% of all members; if quorum exists, a motion passes when yes votes are strictly more than no votes.
First test quorum using all members as the denominator. Only then compare yes and no; abstentions count for presence but not as no votes under this rule.
Is quorum met, and does the motion pass?
1. Quorum threshold=ceil(0.60×23)=14. 2. Present=23, so quorum is met. 3. Yes=11, no=11; yes>no is False. 4. Combine the two tests.
Quorum is met; the motion does not pass.
Procedural reasoning requires applying tests in the right order and using the correct denominator.
Threshold predicates: quorum(present,total) and majority(yes,no); pass = quorum ∧ majority.

Representation can be modeled by rules that convert population into seats. Different allocation rules can produce different results, so the rule must be stated.

Three districts have populations A=120, B=120, C=60. They must share 14 seats. Use this stated method: compute each exact quota population/total×seats; give each district the whole-number part; assign remaining seats to the largest fractional remainders.
Use only the stated largest-remainder method. Seat totals must add exactly to the available number.
How many seats does each district receive?

1. Total population=300. 2. Exact quotas: A=5.60, B=5.60, C=2.80. 3. Initial whole seats: [5, 5, 2], leaving 2. 4. Give the remaining seat(s) to the largest remainder(s). 5. Final allocation=[5, 6, 3], which sums to 14.
Fair representation is not just arithmetic; it depends on an explicit apportionment procedure.
Largest-remainder apportionment: quotas, floors, then rank fractional remainders.
